column2: Ukiyo-e woodblock print (Hokusai, Hiroshige). The glass is a print: flat colour blocks printed from separate woodblocks, crisp sumi keylines, Prussian blue, vermilion, pale persimmon, sky with bokashi (the printer's hand-wiped gradation, the medium's one allowed gradient, dithered), visible washi paper fibre, a red cartouche with the title and a seal in a carved script you draw. The numerals belong to the scene the way Hokusai's waves and Mount Fuji do: a great wave whose claws curl into digits, a Fuji whose snowcap outline traces a numeral, a bridge and travellers, pines bent in wind... design all ten so they read first as digits but are clearly carved and printed. Restrained effects: the wave's foam fingers flicker; a flock of birds rolls through the sky in a slow wave; rain lines (Hiroshige's sudden shower) slide diagonally for a while; a soft sheen of mica ground (kirazuri) glints along the sky. Minute turn: the print is made block by block: the old digit's colour blocks lift off one by one as fresh paper shows (before :00), and the new digit is printed after :00: keyblock line first, then each colour block presses down in register with a small offset settle. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the season changes (a colour front sweeps the print from summer to snow or cherry blossom) while the keylines stay. Strictly flat woodblock colour with its own textures.

Leaded stained glass. The glass becomes a church window: pieces of pot-metal coloured glass (ruby, cobalt, emerald, gold, amber, violet) held in thick dark lead cames, with painted grisaille lines on some pieces and the irregular streaks of real antique glass. The numerals are made of glass pieces: each digit a run of pieces in one family of colour inside its own lead outline, designed as leaded shapes (cames meet at angles, pieces are cut convex) that read first as digits, set into a window of quarries, borders and a rose or tracery. Restrained effects: light from outside moves: a slow soft beam of sunlight crosses the window so pieces glow brighter as it passes (a flat brightness change per piece, never 3D), the odd piece twinkles, a cloud shadow drifts across, coloured light pooled on the sill below. Minute turn: a glazier works in the window: the old digit's pieces are knocked out of their lead and fall as flat shards (gone before :00), and new pieces are set and the lead closed around them after :00, each piece lighting up as the sun reaches it. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the sun moves through the day: dawn to noon to sunset colours sweep the window, at night the window goes dark from outside and is lit from inside by candles. Flat glass and lead only.

A metro map (Harry Beck's London Tube diagram, Vignelli's New York). The glass is a transit diagram: thick flat coloured lines at 0/45/90 degrees with rounded corners, white station ticks and interchange rings, a river in pale blue, the map's own sans lettering for station names and a line key, in a clean typeface you draw. The numerals are drawn by the lines themselves: each digit is a line's route with its 45-degree bends, loops and termini, one line colour per digit, interchanges where digits touch. Restrained effects: little trains glide along every line, stopping at stations and accelerating away; stations glow softly as a train calls; a 'you are here' dot pulses; a service-change banner slides by. Minute turn: the old line is closed: its stations grey out and its track fades along the route from one terminus to the other (gone before :00); a new line is built after :00, its colour drawn out along the new route from a terminus with the trains following, stations opening one by one. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the map redraws as a night-service map (the Night Tube) or the whole network re-colours in a sweep, the time readable throughout. Flat diagram only.

Byzantine gold mosaic (Ravenna, Hagia Sophia). Every pixel or 2x2 is a tessera: smalti glass in deep blues, greens, reds, and a gold-leaf ground set at slightly different angles, with the dark grout lines and the 'andamento' (rows of tesserae flowing along each shape's contours). The numerals are set in tesserae the way the craftsmen set halos and lettering: rows of tesserae following the digit's stroke, outlined in a dark row, against the shimmering gold ground, designed as a set of ten that read first as digits, maybe with a Byzantine letterform flavour you draw. Restrained effects: the gold ground glitters: because the tesserae are tilted, a slow travelling glint makes individual tesserae flash and go dark (a few pixels at a time, sparkling across like candlelight), a candle flicker modulates the gold, peacocks or doves in the borders shift. Minute turn: the mosaicist sets the new digit tessera by tessera along the andamento, in flowing rows (after :00), the old digit's tesserae having dropped out in a scatter to show the grey setting bed (before :00). Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the whole apse catches the sunrise, a wave of glints rolls through all the gold, or the setting bed is laid fresh and a new band of ornament is set. Flat tesserae, glitter only from the gold's tilt.

Paper marbling (Turkish ebru / Japanese suminagashi). The glass is the size bath seen from above: flat floating colours (indigo, oxblood, ochre, turquoise, black, white) dropped on the surface and combed into patterns: stone, nonpareil, bouquet, feathers. The numerals are drawn in the floating paint with a stylus: each digit a line of dropped colour that the comb then drags into the marbled field's own feathered texture, so the digits are made of the same flowing bands but in a contrasting colour family with a white 'moat' of size around them, designed so all ten read first as digits. Always alive: the surface drifts and slowly swirls (paint advected by a smooth flow field: precompute it, the bands move at sub-pixel speed), new drops bloom as expanding rings, and a restrained effect or two: a light reflection sliding across the wet surface, a ripple when a drop lands. Minute turn: the stylus or comb drags the old digit into the background pattern so it dissolves into feathers (before :00), and a new digit is dropped and drawn in fresh paint after :00. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the marbler lays a sheet of paper on the bath and lifts it, taking the whole pattern away as a print, and a fresh bath is sprinkled with the new hour drawn at once. Flat floating colour only. Mind cost: advect via precomputed lookup tables, not per-pixel simulation.

Delftware tiles. The glass is a wall of white tin-glazed tiles painted in cobalt blue (one or two blues and a hint of manganese purple), each tile with its corner motifs ('ox-head' or 'spider' corners) and a centre scene: windmills, ships, children's games, tulips, a Dutch skater. The numerals are painted across tiles in the Delft painter's brushwork: blue line and wash, a bold contour with lighter wash inside, designed as a set of ten flowing brushed digits in an old Dutch letterform you draw. Restrained effects: the glaze catches light: a slow soft reflection slides across the wall tile by tile (a flat sheen band, each tile's glaze slightly different), the windmill sails turn, a little ship sails across a tile and into the next, a skater glides tile to tile. Minute turn: the old digit's tiles are prised out one by one (gone before :00), revealing plaster, and new painted tiles slide or drop in after :00, each painted digit fragment visible on its tile as it lands. Or the painter's brush paints the digit stroke by stroke on fresh tiles. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the tiles flip over in a wave to show a new set of scenes (a winter set, a harbour set), the digits re-painted, time readable throughout. Flat blue paint on white glaze; the sheen is the only effect allowed beyond the painting.

Tangram. The seven flat pieces (two big triangles, a medium triangle, two small, a square, a parallelogram) in a set of bright colours, on a felt or wooden table ground. Each digit is a tangram figure assembled from its own seven pieces (all seven, as the puzzle requires), designed so all ten read first as digits; or use two sets per digit if needed for legibility; the pieces' crisp edges and 45-degree geometry are the letterform. Always alive: pieces breathe and settle by tiny slides, a shadowless flat play; restrained effects: a slow light sweep across the lacquered pieces, a soft colour pulse through the set, the parallelogram flipping (a flat flip) now and then in an idle hum. Minute turn: the old figure's pieces slide and rotate (pieces may rotate, but never the shown digit) out of the digit into a neat stacked square at the edge (before :00) and then fly in a smooth choreography to their places in the new digit (after :00), so the reader only sees half-assembled shapes that are not another digit. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. all 28 pieces assemble into a tangram picture (a cat, a boat, a running man) and burst apart into the new hour. Flat coloured pieces only, AA edges allowed because the pieces are big clean shapes.

Weather radar. The glass is a radar reflectivity map in the honest NWS palette (light green, green, yellow, orange, red, magenta for hail), over a dark flat basemap of county lines, rivers and a coastline, with the radar's overlay: range rings, a rotating sweep line from the radar site, a timestamp, a dBZ legend, a storm-track arrow, in a small instrument font you draw. The numerals are storm cells: each digit a squall line or supercell whose reflectivity bands make the numeral (hottest core in the middle of each stroke, rings of decreasing colour bands outward, flat colour steps, no shading), with a hook echo on one digit and a bow echo on another. Always alive: the storms drift along their track at sub-pixel speed, the sweep line rotates (each pass refreshes the echo, as real radar does), small showers bloom and fade around the digits, lightning strike marks flash; restrained effects: the sweep's faint afterglow, a gentle flicker of the cores. Minute turn: the old cell decays: its colour bands step down the palette and break up (gone before :00); the new cell grows in from its core after :00, each sweep pass adding a band. Hour: a bigger show, e.g. the radar switches products (velocity mode red-green, then back), or a warning polygon is drawn and the whole line sweeps through, time readable. Flat false-colour bands through a lookup table.
